Day 1
From Hotel: 5 min · 2 min → Harpa Concert Hall
1. Harpa Concert Hall
Award-winning glass-and-steel concert hall on the waterfront, designed with Ólafur Elíasson's honeycomb facade. Freely walkable interior with harbour views and acoustic architecture worth exploring even without a show.

8 min · 3 min → Sun Voyager
2. Sun Voyager
Jón Gunnar Árnason's stainless-steel "dreamboat" on the Sæbraut waterfront, unveiled in 1990 for Reykjavík's 200th anniversary. Often mistaken for a Viking ship, the artist meant it as an ode to the sun — a promise of undiscovered territory and hope.

17 min · 5 min → Old Harbour
3. Old Harbour & Grandagarður
Reykjavík's working old harbour, lined with fishing boats, street art murals, and the Grandi district's converted warehouses — now home to food halls, artist studios, and whale-watching piers. Free to explore at any pace.

4. Viðey Island
Reykjavík's largest offshore island, a short ferry crossing from the mainland — 10th-century archaeological remains, Videyjarstofa · Iceland's oldest stone house, dated 1755 · Richard Serra's basalt sculpture walk Áfangar, and Yoko Ono's Imagine Peace Tower.

From Hotel: 7 min · 3 min → Hallgrímskirkja
1. Hallgrímskirkja
Iceland's tallest building and most recognisable landmark — a concrete expressionist church whose 74-metre tower offers a 360° panorama over the city and Faxaflói Bay. The Leif Eriksson statue stands at the entrance.

2. Sundhöllin Swimming Pool
Reykjavík's oldest public pool, designed by Guðjón Samúelsson in 1937 and fully renovated in 2017 — geothermal hot pots, an outdoor pool, and local swimming culture at its most authentic and unhurried.

3. Tjörnin & Hljómskálagarður
Reykjavík's tidal-turned-freshwater pond in the heart of downtown, ringed by City Hall and the sculpture-dotted lawns of Hljómskálagarður park. More than 40 bird species nest along its shores, and the surface freezes for skating in winter.

8 min · 3 min → Christ the King Cathedral
4. Christ the King Cathedral
Iceland's only Catholic cathedral — locally Landakotskirkja — a Gothic Revival basilica in white-painted concrete designed by Guðjón Samúelsson, the same architect behind Hallgrímskirkja, and consecrated in 1929. Twin square towers crown the hilltop Landakot site.

Day 3
From Hotel: 47 min → Þingvellir National Park
1. Þingvellir National Park
A rift-valley national park on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge where the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart. Site of Iceland's Alþing parliament founded in 930, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2004.
Read more
Open 24/7
~1.5 hr
Þingvellir National Park
50 min → Geysir & Strokkur
2. Geysir & Strokkur
An active geothermal field in the Haukadalur valley with hot springs, mud pools and fumaroles. The fountain geyser Strokkur erupts every 6 to 10 minutes to 15 to 20 metres, beside the dormant Great Geysir that named all geysers.
Read more
Open 24/7
~1 hr
Geysir Geothermal Area
13 min → Gullfoss
3. Gullfoss
The "Golden Falls" — a two-tiered waterfall on the glacial Hvítá river dropping 11 metres then 21 metres into a canyon up to 70 metres deep. Saved from hydroelectric development and protected as a conservation site since 1979.
Read more
Open 24/7
~1 hr
Gullfoss
52 min → Kerið
4. Kerið
A volcanic crater lake in the Grímsnes area, formed roughly 6,500 years ago. The caldera is about 55 metres deep, with walls of red volcanic rock encircling vivid blue-green water.

1. Seljalandsfoss
A 60-metre waterfall on the Seljalands river, fed by meltwater from the Eyjafjallajökull glacier-volcano. A footpath leads behind the falling water — one of few waterfalls in the world offering this view.

2. Skógafoss
A 60-metre-high, 25-metre-wide waterfall on the Skógá river in the village of Skógar. A staircase climbs to a viewing platform at the top, and the spray frequently throws rainbows across the falls on sunny days.

3. Dyrhólaey
A 120-metre promontory and nature reserve forming Iceland's southernmost point, named for the large sea-eroded arch in its headland. Puffins nest on the cliffs from May to August, and a lighthouse crowns the summit.

A black-sand beach near Vík backed by basalt columns and the Hálsanefshellir cave, with the Reynisdrangar sea stacks offshore. Powerful sneaker waves make the surf zone dangerous — a warning-light system marks restricted areas.

From Hotel: 2h 20min → Búðakirkja
1. Búðakirkja
An iconic black wooden church in the hamlet of Búðir, set in the Búðahraun lava field on the south coast of Snæfellsnes. The current church dates to 1848; its pitch-painted timber against the lava is among the most photographed in Iceland.

2. Arnarstapi
A small fishing village on the southern side of Snæfellsnes, within Snæfellsjökull National Park. Known for dramatic basalt sea cliffs, the Gatklettur stone arch, summer seabird colonies, and a coastal trail to neighbouring Hellnar.

3. Djúpalónssandur
A black-pebble beach within Snæfellsjökull National Park at the foot of the glacier. It holds four historic fishermen's lifting stones once used to test crew strength, and the rusted iron remains of the British trawler Epine, wrecked here in 1948.

A highland canyon lined with dozens of slender waterfalls cascading over moss-covered cliffs into a blue-green river, earning it the nickname Valley of Tears. The flow was reduced after the Sigalda hydropower plant opened in 1978.

Local Tastes
Pylsur — The Icelandic Hot Dog
A lamb-and-pork hot dog topped with raw onion, crispy fried onion, ketchup, sweet mustard · pylsusinnep, and remoulade. The bun is steamed. Bill Clinton ordered one without onions in 2004; the stand still has the sign.
Bæjarins Beztu Pylsur
Skyr
Iceland's ancient dairy product — thick, mild, high-protein, and closer to strained yoghurt than cheese. Eaten as breakfast with berries and cream, or as a dessert. Icelanders have eaten it for over a thousand years.
Café Loki
Kleinur
Iceland's traditional twisted doughnut — a fried pastry dusted in sugar, lighter than a German Berliner, with a distinct cardamom-tinged flavour. Found in every bakery and petrol station across the country.
Sandholt Bakery
Hangikjöt
Slow-smoked lamb, traditionally smoked over sheep dung and birch. The smoke is deep and complex; the meat is tender and slightly gamey. Served cold in thin slices on flatbread · flatkaka, or hot with potatoes and white sauce.
Matur og Drykkur
Kjötsúpa — Lamb Soup
Iceland's national soup — bone-in lamb simmered for hours with root vegetables · turnip, rutabaga, carrot, potato and pearl barley. Thick, warming, and deeply savoury. The standard winter meal for a thousand years.
Café Loki
Food Delivery
Wolt
Foreign number: accepted — any mobile number that can receive an SMS code works.
Reykjavik's dominant delivery platform with solid coverage of the city centre. Selection is smaller than in a major capital but includes most restaurants around Laugavegur and the Old Town area.

Getting Around
Hreyfill
Foreign number: not accepted — an Icelandic phone number is required to register.
Reykjavik's main taxi app. International visitors cannot register through the app; hail from the street or ask the hotel to call one. Reliable and metered.

Worth Knowing

A 41-Year Church, A Longhouse Found by Accident

Hallgrímskirkja's rippled concrete facade was designed to echo Iceland's basalt columns — the hexagonal rock formations that form when lava cools slowly, the same shapes you'll see later at waterfalls and sea cliffs around the country. Architect Guðjón Samúelsson drew up the design in 1937, but the building itself took 41 years to finish: construction started in 1945, the crypt was consecrated in 1948, the tower and wings went up by 1974, and the main nave wasn't finally consecrated until 1986 — meaning most Icelanders who watched the tower rise as children were adults with children of their own by the time the church was actually complete.

Viðey was farmed for centuries and then, within a generation, it wasn't — the island was abandoned in the 1940s and no one has lived there since. What remains is a strange layering of eras on one small island: a 13th-century Augustinian monastery site, Videyjarstofa · built in 1755, the oldest stone house in Iceland · and, since 2007, Yoko Ono's Imagine Peace Tower, a beam of light dedicated to John Lennon that's switched on every year between his birthday and the anniversary of his death. Richard Serra's nine pairs of basalt columns, installed across the island in 1990, are easy to miss entirely if you don't know to look for them against the horizon.
